Hi Ava — great to meet you and glad the demo was useful. Attaching a one-page rate card and a small CSV with worked token-count examples (Brightline_ratecard_v1.pdf; token-count-examples.csv).

Below is a concise, plain-language explanation you can drop into the SOW. If procurement wants us to include this as an appendix we can also provide a one-paragraph blurb for the SOW itself.

Token counting — short explanation (for SOW):
- Prompt (input) tokens: everything that you send to the model at request time is counted as input tokens. This includes user messages, system prompts, and any explicit function/tool invocation text that is provided in the request payload.
- Completion (output) tokens: tokens generated by the model (assistant) are billed as output tokens. For function/tool calls where the tool returns content to the model, that tooling output is billed as assistant output tokens if the tool output is emitted back to the client; if the tool output is then included in a subsequent request from the client, it will be billed again as input tokens in that subsequent request.
- Streaming: we bill output tokens as they are generated/streamed to the client. There is no wait-for-complete behavior — partial streamed tokens are counted as output when emitted.
- Rounding/granularity: Redwood bills actual token counts; we do not round upward to fixed blocks per individual request. Invoice lines sum token usage across the billing period; per-request counts are exact to the token. (Note: some add-on features such as fine-grained embedding microbatches may have minimum billing thresholds — we can call these out explicitly in the SOW if needed.)

A couple of quick examples are included in the CSV attachment so you can put sample lines on an invoice. For Brightline's volume (~4M tokens/mo) the hosted API baseline pricing in the attached rate card would estimate a monthly charge of $X (see the example rows). Committed spend discounts and multi-month commitments can reduce the effective rate — happy to propose a 12-month committed package if procurement prefers a predictable unit price.

Next steps: if this looks good I can loop in our finance rep and get a draft SOW/appendix to you this week. Shall I schedule a 20-min call with James + your engineering lead?

--- draft to client (compact answers) ---
Q1 — end-to-end example (system + tool + assistant):
- You send a request that includes a 36‑token system prompt + user message = 36 input tokens.
- The model makes a function/tool call; the tool emits 120 tokens of structured JSON. That 120 tokens are considered assistant output tokens if the tool output is returned to the client as part of the response. If the tool output is only used internally and not emitted back to the client, it's still counted as assistant output if generated by the model/tool, because it was produced in the response stream.
- The assistant then emits a 20‑token human-readable reply. That 20 tokens are assistant output tokens as well.
- If the tool output is then included by the client in a subsequent request, those tokens will be billed again as input tokens in that later request.

So, in the above logical transaction you should expect: Input = 36 tokens; Output = 120 + 20 = 140 tokens.

Q2 — streaming cancellation:
- You are billed for output tokens as they are emitted to the client. If you cancel the stream after 40 tokens have been emitted, you are billed for the 40 emitted tokens only. There is no additional per-request rounding up applied by default.

Q3 — tool/internal-only outputs: 
- If the tool produces output that is generated as part of the response cycle (regardless of whether it is returned to the end-user), we treat that as assistant output and bill it accordingly. The only time those tokens would not be billed as output is if they are never materialized/emitted by the runtime (for example, truncated before generation).

Notes on rounding and minimums:
- We report exact token counts per request and aggregate them for invoice periods. We do not apply a per-request rounding-up increment. There are some optional features (e.g., dedicated microbatch embedding bundles) that have minimum billing blocks; we will call those out separately if applicable to your use case.
